VeriCUA: Learning Proactive Verification for
Reliable GUI Agent Rewards

Zhizhou Wang ††thanks: Equal contribution (jenojeff66@gmail.com, lyx23@mails.tsinghua.edu.cn). Affiliation: Southwest Jiaotong University    Yaxi Lu11footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: Tsinghua University    Zhong Zhang ††thanks: Corresponding author (zhong.zhang@uestc.edu.cn, fangminghk@gmail.com). Affiliation: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China    Zikun Hu Affiliation: National University of Singapore    Xin Cong Affiliation: Tsinghua University    Yankai Lin Affiliation: Renmin University of China    Fangming Liu22footnotemark: 2 Affiliation: Peng Cheng Laboratory
Abstract

Reinforcement learning for computer-use agents increasingly relies on proactive reward agents that interact with the post-execution GUI environment to verify what recorded screenshots cannot reveal. The reliability of such verification hinges on two coupled decisions: what to check and when to stop. Existing methods leave these decisions to prompted foundation models. However, neither scaling up the model nor providing few-shot examples reliably improves verification: prompted Judges ranging from 4B to GPT-5.4 all plateau at 68%68\%–70%70\% macro-average agreement. This is because the value of a check depends on the environment rather than the task alone, and becomes apparent only through execution. Learning from execution is itself constrained, as the Actor’s terminal state cannot be faithfully replicated during training, allowing only one verification attempt per state. We introduce VeriCUA, a proactive reward agent that learns its verification strategy from these single attempts. A trainable Judge decides what to check and when to stop, while a frozen Probe executes the checks in the live environment. Online reinforcement learning optimizes the Judge for both verdict correctness and efficient Probe use, with returns normalized across terminal states. Trained only on OSWorld and evaluated without further training on MobileWorld and WebArena-Verified, VeriCUA achieves the highest reward agreement across all three benchmarks and lies on the agreement–cost Pareto frontier among proactive verifiers. It surpasses few-shot GPT-5.4 by 5.365.36 points with 47.6%47.6\%–59.8%59.8\% fewer Probe tokens, and even a 1B VeriCUA exceeds every prompted Judge. As the reward for Actor RL, it raises task success by 3.213.21 points overall and 5.405.40 points on held-out multi-application tasks. These results identify the verification strategy, not verifier scale, as the key to reliable GUI rewards. Code is available at https://github.com/Jeffjeno/VeriCUA.

1 Introduction

Training computer-use agents (CUAs) with reinforcement learning requires reliable rewards for task completion (Lv et al., 2026; Lai et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026). Rule-based rewards are precise but brittle and difficult to scale (Xie et al., 2024; El Hattami et al., 2025; Kong et al., 2026), while passive model-based rewards are more flexible but can only verify what is exposed in the available observations (Qi et al., 2025; Bai et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025). Decisive evidence, such as the contents of a saved file or other hidden application state, may therefore remain unobserved (Cai et al., 2025). Proactive verification addresses this limitation by interacting with the post-execution environment to acquire the missing evidence before issuing a verdict (Dai et al., 2026; Cui et al., 2026; Shi et al., 2026). Because such verification is performed for every training rollout, it must be not only accurate but also efficient enough to avoid invoking an expensive model for each reward.

Interaction alone, however, does not guarantee a reliable verdict. Reliability depends on the verification strategy, which consists of two coupled decisions the task leaves open: what to check and when to stop. For a task that requires notes on every slide, one slide without notes already establishes failure (Figure 1(b)). The prompted verifier in Figure 1(a) instead requests a slide-by-slide comparison and keeps scrolling without reaching a verdict. Scale does not fix this. Under the same verification loop, prompted Judges from a 4B model to GPT-5.4 all reach 68%68\%–70%70\% macro-average agreement, and few-shot examples add at most 0.60.6 points (Table 1).

Our key observation is that a check’s value is revealed by executing it, not by reading the task. A prompted Judge sees the task and the recorded screenshots, which show what a plausible check looks like but not what evidence it will return. That depends on where the evidence resides, the state the Actor left, and what the Probe can reach. When to stop depends on how often screenshot-only verdicts turn out to be correct. The strategy must therefore be learned by executing verification and comparing its verdicts with true outcomes.

Learning from execution, however, faces a single-attempt constraint: each Actor terminal state admits only one verification attempt, which rules out within-state rollout comparisons. An Actor starts from a resettable initial state, so RL can compare several rollouts from the same state (Shao et al., 2024). A GUI verifier starts from the Actor’s terminal state, the product of one stochastic execution. Re-execution may not reproduce it, identical screenshots can hide different application state, and probing itself changes it.

We introduce VeriCUA, a proactive GUI reward agent that learns its verification strategy under this constraint. A trainable Judge decides what to check and when to stop, and a frozen GUI Probe executes the checks. Freezing the Probe ties outcome differences to the Judge and lets the Probe be swapped without retraining. We initialize the Judge with outcome-filtered teacher traces and then train it with online RL on complete attempts graded by executable outcomes, so each check is credited by the evidence it actually yields. The reward also depends on whether the Probe was used, which lets a single attempt signal whether stopping was right. Returns are normalized across terminal states in each batch (Hu et al., 2025), so no environment forking is required.

We evaluate VeriCUA on OSWorld (Xie et al., 2024), MobileWorld (Kong et al., 2026), and WebArena-Verified (El Hattami et al., 2025). First, strategy matters more than scale. VeriCUA surpasses few-shot GPT-5.4 by 5.365.36 macro-average points with 47.6%47.6\%–59.8%59.8\% fewer Probe tokens and lies on the agreement–cost Pareto frontier (Figure 4). Even VeriCUA-1B outperforms prompted GPT-5.4 (OpenAI, 2026) and its teacher Kimi-K2.6 (Kimi, 2026). Second, the learned strategy transfers. Trained only on OSWorld, the Judge achieves the highest agreement on unseen mobile and web environments. Third, better rewards train better agents. VeriCUA rewards raise downstream Pass@4 by 3.213.21 points overall and by 5.405.40 points on held-out MultiApp tasks.

2 Method

2.1 Overview

As shown in Figure 2, VeriCUA verifies the Actor’s task outcome using its execution history and live terminal environment. It consists of a trainable Judge and a frozen GUI Probe. The Judge initially formulates task-success checks and marks each as satisfied, violated, or unresolved based on the available evidence. If the evidence supports a success or failure verdict, verification terminates. Otherwise, subject to the probing budget, the Probe gathers evidence for the unresolved checks and returns status updates with supporting observations. Subsequent Judge calls retain the checks from the previous round and update their statuses using the returned evidence.

By specifying what the Probe inspects and deciding whether to request further interaction, the Judge determines the evidence acquired and hence the verdict. We train it on complete verification attempts, one per Actor terminal state, with a reward on verdict correctness and Probe use (Sections 2.3 and 2.4).

2.2 The Judge-Probe Verification Loop

Consider an Actor policy πθ\pi_{\theta} attempting task xx in a live GUI environment ℰ\mathcal{E} and terminating at time TT with trajectory τ=(o0,a0,…,aT−1,oT)\tau=(o_{0},a_{0},\ldots,a_{T-1},o_{T}), where oto_{t} and ata_{t} denote GUI observations and actions. The Judge receives xx and an input representation ψ⁡(τ)\psi(\tau) containing the Actor’s action history and its most recent screenshots (Appendix I). When the Judge requests additional evidence, the frozen Probe interacts with the live terminal environment to inspect unresolved task conditions and returns status updates with supporting observations. Each round therefore involves the two decisions that make up the verification strategy: whether the current evidence supports a terminal verdict and, if not, which checks to send to the Probe.

Judge.

Let ℋ(k)\mathcal{H}^{(k)} denote the verification history available to the Judge at call kk, consisting of the initial Actor input and the checks and Probe evidence retained from earlier rounds. At call k∈{0,…,K}k\in\{0,\ldots,K\}, where KK is the maximum number of Probe invocations, the trainable Judge JϕJ_{\phi} conditions on the task xx and ℋ(k)\mathcal{H}^{(k)} to produce a verdict and status-annotated checks:

(v(k),C(k))=Jϕ​(x,ℋ(k)),ℋ(0)=ψ⁡(τ).\bigl(v^{(k)},C^{(k)}\bigr)=J_{\phi}\!\left(x,\mathcal{H}^{(k)}\right),\qquad\mathcal{H}^{(0)}=\psi(\tau). (1)

Here v(k)∈{success,failure,uncertain}v^{(k)}\in\{\texttt{success},\texttt{failure},\texttt{uncertain}\}, and C(k)C^{(k)} pairs each check with a status: satisfied, violated, or unresolved. The check text is generated at k=0k=0 and the statuses are updated thereafter. The Judge returns success when all checks are satisfied, failure when any is violated, and uncertain otherwise. A success or failure verdict terminates verification. When v(k)=uncertainv^{(k)}=\texttt{uncertain} and k<Kk<K, only the unresolved subset Cu(k)⊆C(k)C_{u}^{(k)}\subseteq C^{(k)} is passed to the Probe.

Probe.

The frozen Probe PP gathers evidence for the unresolved checks in the current live environment. We keep it frozen so that differences in verification outcome are attributable to the Judge. Its instructions confine it to inspecting the environment, without completing or repairing the Actor’s task (Appendix I). Its interaction trajectory and returned evidence are represented as

(τP(k),e(k))∼P(⋅∣Cu(k);ℰ(k)),ℋ(k+1)=ℋ(k)⊕(C(k),e(k)).\bigl(\tau_{P}^{(k)},e^{(k)}\bigr)\sim P\!\left(\cdot\mid C_{u}^{(k)};\mathcal{E}^{(k)}\right),\qquad\mathcal{H}^{(k+1)}=\mathcal{H}^{(k)}\oplus\bigl(C^{(k)},e^{(k)}\bigr). (2)

Here ℰ(0)\mathcal{E}^{(0)} is the Actor’s terminal environment, and each subsequent Probe invocation continues from the state reached by the preceding Probe actions. The returned evidence e(k)e^{(k)} comprises check-status updates and selected supporting observations, and ⊕\oplus denotes concatenation. Only e(k)e^{(k)} reaches the Judge; the full Probe trace τP(k)\tau_{P}^{(k)} does not, and each invocation starts without the interaction history of earlier rounds, so neither component’s context grows with the other’s execution length.

2.3 Outcome Feedback from a Single Attempt

We assign a terminal reward to each complete verification attempt, combining verdict correctness with whether probing was used. A correctness-only reward scores a correct verdict reached directly the same as one reached after probing. Because each terminal state admits a single attempt, there is no sibling attempt to reveal whether probing was needed, so the reward itself must carry that signal.

Let Y^i\hat{Y}_{i} denote the final Judge verdict and YiY_{i} the executable outcome recorded before Probe interaction. We set pi=1p_{i}=1 if the verification attempt invokes the Probe at least once, and pi=0p_{i}=0 otherwise, so the probing term of the reward reflects the Judge’s stopping decision rather than the frozen Probe’s execution length. The terminal reward is ri=R⁡(Y^i,Yi,pi)r_{i}=R(\hat{Y}_{i},Y_{i},p_{i}).

Correct verdicts receive higher rewards when reached without probing, encouraging reliable judgments from existing evidence. Incorrect verdicts receive larger penalties when issued without probing, discouraging premature judgments. Unresolved or invalid outputs receive the lowest reward, discouraging attempts that exhaust the probing budget without reaching a terminal verdict. The exact reward schedule is given in Appendix G.

We use this terminal reward to jointly train check formulation and stop-or-probe decisions over verification attempts. The reward preferences teach the Judge to stop once the evidence suffices, while the shared return trains check formulation through its effect on the evidence collected and the verdict. We next describe how we collect verification trajectories and optimize the Judge.

2.4 Online Optimization of the Judge

Initialization.

Before online optimization, we initialize the Judge by supervised fine-tuning on teacher verification trajectories whose final verdicts match the executable outcomes. These traces provide examples of structured check generation and verdict prediction, so that each attempt during online RL is a complete, well-formed verification. The Probe remains frozen.

Sampling verification trajectories.

We run the Judge from the live terminal environment of each Actor rollout and execute its Probe requests to obtain the evidence. Each completed verification attempt receives the terminal reward defined in Section 2.3. Unlike an Actor’s resettable initial state, this terminal environment is produced by one stochastic execution: replaying the Actor need not reproduce it, transient state such as unsaved edits and modal dialogs cannot be confirmed from screenshots, and Probe actions further alter it. We therefore collect one verification trajectory per Actor terminal environment, without environment forking or same-state verifier rollout groups.

Updating the Judge.

We optimize the Judge with REINFORCE++ (Hu et al., 2025), which normalizes terminal returns across the independent terminal environments in each batch. Let zi=((vi(0),Ci(0)),ei(0),…,(vi(Ki),Ci(Ki)))z_{i}=\bigl((v_{i}^{(0)},C_{i}^{(0)}),e_{i}^{(0)},\ldots,(v_{i}^{(K_{i})},C_{i}^{(K_{i})})\bigr) denote a complete verification trajectory with Ki≤KK_{i}\leq K Probe invocations and terminal reward rir_{i}. When Ki=0K_{i}=0, the trajectory contains only the initial Judge output. For a batch ℬ\mathcal{B} of complete verification trajectories, the normalized return supplies the advantage for every active Judge token:

Ai,k,t=ri−μℬσℬ2+ϵ,(i,k,t)∈𝒜ℬ.A_{i,k,t}=\frac{r_{i}-\mu_{\mathcal{B}}}{\sqrt{\sigma_{\mathcal{B}}^{2}+\epsilon}},\qquad(i,k,t)\in\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{B}}. (3)

Here μℬ\mu_{\mathcal{B}} and σℬ2\sigma_{\mathcal{B}}^{2} are the mean and variance of terminal rewards in the batch, and ϵ>0\epsilon>0 ensures numerical stability. The index set 𝒜ℬ\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{B}} contains active Judge tokens, indexed by trajectory ii, Judge call kk, and token position tt. Only newly generated Judge tokens contribute to the loss; context tokens and Probe outputs are excluded. The following log-probability surrogate expresses the on-policy gradient at the rollout policy:

ℒJudge(ϕ)=−1|𝒜ℬ|∑(i,k,t)∈𝒜ℬAi,k,tlogπϕJ(yi,k,t∣hi,k,t),\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Judge}}(\phi)=-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{B}}|}\sum_{(i,k,t)\in\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{B}}}A_{i,k,t}\log\pi_{\phi}^{J}\left(y_{i,k,t}\mid h_{i,k,t}\right), (4)

where πϕJ\pi_{\phi}^{J} is the autoregressive Judge policy, yi,k,ty_{i,k,t} is the generated token, and hi,k,th_{i,k,t} is its conditioning context. The loss averages over active Judge tokens across the batch. For parameter updates, we use the clipped likelihood-ratio objective described in Appendix E, with rollout-policy probabilities and normalized returns held fixed.

Using the trained verifier.

After training, we freeze VeriCUA and map its final verdict to a binary reward r^i=𝕀[VeriCUA (xi,τi,ℰiT)=success]\hat{r}_{i}=\mathbb{I}\!\left[\textsc{VeriCUA }{}(x_{i},\tau_{i},\mathcal{E}_{i}^{T})=\texttt{success}\right], where ℰiT\mathcal{E}_{i}^{T} is the terminal environment of Actor rollout ii. We keep VeriCUA fixed and optimize the Actor with vanilla GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), grouping Actor rollouts generated from the same task initialization. Each rollout is verified once from its own terminal environment, and the resulting verdict determines its reward r^i\hat{r}_{i}.

3 Experiments

Our experiments examine whether a learned verification strategy improves reward agreement over prompted verifiers across model scales and at what Probe cost, whether it generalizes beyond its training environment, and whether the resulting rewards improve downstream Actor learning.

3.1 Experimental Setup

Benchmarks.

We evaluate on the OSWorld (Xie et al., 2024) tasks that require neither network access nor Google Drive, the GUI-only subset of MobileWorld (Kong et al., 2026), and WebArena-Verified Hard (El Hattami et al., 2025), using 414414, 100100, and 100100 trajectories, respectively. These cover successful executions and diverse failures from five Actors: EvoCUA-32B (Xue et al., 2026), Qwen3.8-27B (Qwen Team, 2026), Holo3.1-35B-A3B (H Company, 2026), Qwen3-VL-4B-Thinking (Bai et al., 2025), and Gemini 3.7 Flash (Google DeepMind, 2026). Each trajectory includes the action–observation history, the clean task snapshot from which its terminal environment can be re-executed, and an executable outcome label hidden from all verifiers.

Training data.

We train the Judge only on OSWorld and keep it frozen thereafter, so MobileWorld and WebArena-Verified test zero-shot transfer. Each environment uses one frozen Probe shared by all VeriCUA variants. We denote trained Judges by size: VeriCUA-4B (Qwen3-VL-4B-Thinking), VeriCUA-2B (Qwen3-VL-2B-Thinking), and VeriCUA-1B (MiniCPM-V-4.6-Thinking (Yu et al., 2026; Yao et al., 2024)). SFT uses Kimi-K2.6 verification traces and online RL uses newly collected OSWorld trajectories, all disjoint from evaluation (Appendix G).

Baselines.

Unless noted, all baselines use Qwen3-VL-4B-Thinking, and existing methods follow their published observation and prompting configurations (Appendix D). (i) Passive verifiers: DistRL (Wang et al., 2025), DigiRL (Bai et al., 2024), and ZeroGUI (Yang et al., 2025). (ii) Prompted proactive verifiers: VAGEN (Cui et al., 2026) and prompted VeriCUA, which shares trained VeriCUA’s Judge–Probe architecture, prompts, and budget of at most K=2K{=}2 Probe rounds but uses an off-the-shelf Judge. We also evaluate prompted VeriCUA with the backbones of VeriCUA-2B and VeriCUA-1B, and with the frontier models Kimi-K2.6 and GPT-5.4, both also tested few-shot.

Evaluation protocol.

Both evaluations use the executable task evaluator as ground truth and aggregate four independent runs (Appendix A). Verifier evaluation: We keep only Actor trajectories whose outcome is stable across six re-executions from the clean task snapshot (Appendix D). Each proactive-verifier trial runs in its own re-executed terminal environment, so no verifier’s Probe actions affect another’s. Passive verifiers score the recorded screenshots. We report Avg@44 agreement per benchmark and its unweighted mean (Macro Avg.), and measure cost as frozen-Probe tokens per judgment (Appendix D). Actor evaluation: We train the same Qwen3-VL-4B-Thinking Actor on OSWorld with vanilla GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) under identical tasks, rollout budget, and hyperparameters, varying only the frozen reward source (ZeroGUI, prompted VeriCUA, or trained VeriCUA). We report Pass@44 on the 206206 single-application tasks used for Actor training (ID) and 7474 MultiApp tasks held out from Actor training (OOD).

Implementation details.

We implement Judge SFT with LLaMA-Factory and online RL with Slime, using Megatron Core for parameter updates and SGLang/vLLM for rollout generation with NVIDIA A800 GPUs and Huawei Ascend 910B3 NPUs. Detailed hardware, software, and desktop-environment configurations are provided in Appendix F.

3.2 Verification Strategy Matters More Than Scale

Agreement and Probe-token cost.

Prompted Judges from a 4B model to GPT-5.4 plateau at 68.13%68.13\%–69.62%69.62\% macro-average agreement, and few-shot examples shift this range by at most 1.021.02 points. VeriCUA-4B moves beyond this plateau: it achieves the highest agreement on all three benchmarks (Table 1) and lies on the agreement–cost Pareto frontier of proactive verifiers (Figure 4). Compared with few-shot GPT-5.4, it improves macro-average agreement by 5.365.36 points (68.72%→74.08%68.72\%\rightarrow 74.08\%) with 47.6%47.6\%–59.8%59.8\% fewer Probe tokens. On OSWorld, where GPT-5.4 is strongest, VeriCUA-4B still leads while using 56.9%56.9\% fewer tokens, and its margin widens to 11.2511.25 and 4.254.25 points on MobileWorld and WebArena-Verified. Even VeriCUA-1B (71.62%71.62\%) exceeds every prompted Judge.

Effect of the learned verification policy.

With the Judge backbone, Probe, prompts, and round budget held fixed, training improves agreement on every benchmark. Macro-average agreement rises by 4.504.50, 8.628.62, and 21.1121.11 points over the prompted 4B, 2B, and 1B Judges, respectively, so the gains come from the learned verification policy rather than the architecture. The agreement–cost frontier reflects this: on every benchmark, its highest-agreement point is a trained VeriCUA Judge, and VeriCUA-1B stays on the frontier throughout, dominating every prompted counterpart in both agreement and cost (Figure 4).

3.3 Generality and Behavior of the Learned Strategy

Transfer across environments.

MobileWorld and WebArena-Verified are unseen during training. On both, VeriCUA-4B and VeriCUA-1B, paired with environment-specific Probes, rank first and second, ahead of every prompted and passive verifier including few-shot GPT-5.4. The learned strategy is therefore not specific to desktop applications.

Contribution of training stages.

Figure 5(a) separates SFT initialization from online RL for the Qwen3-VL-4B-Thinking Judge on OSWorld. Agreement rises from 73.73%73.73\% for the prompted Judge to 79.41%79.41\% after SFT and 82.00%82.00\% after online RL, so both stages contribute, with online RL adding 2.592.59 points. Agreement improves on judgments both with and without probing. Every trained Judge also surpasses Kimi-K2.6 (69.62%69.62\% macro average), whose traces initialize it, suggesting that one attempt per terminal state suffices to learn beyond imitation.

Effect of the probing budget.

Figure 5(b) varies the maximum number of Probe rounds for the trained 4B Judge. Agreement increases from 74.09%74.09\% at K=0K{=}0 to 82.00%82.00\% at K=2K{=}2, indicating that evidence from the live environment is decisive. The first round accounts for most of the gain, and two rounds suffice. Because KK only caps interaction, the Judge can still stop earlier.

Robustness to Probe size.

We keep the trained Judge fixed and evaluate Holo3.1 Probes at 35B-A3B, 9B, and 4B scales. OSWorld agreement stays between 82.00%82.00\% and 82.73%82.73\% across these Probes without retraining (Appendix C). This suggests that the learned strategy resides in the Judge, while the Probe mainly executes it.

Evidence acquisition behavior.

We further examine 3333 OSWorld cases in which the recorded Actor trajectory omits outcome-determining evidence that remains accessible through GUI interaction (Appendix B). With the same frozen Probe, VeriCUA-4B directs 61.9%61.9\% of Probe actions toward task-relevant evidence, compared with 47.6%47.6\% for prompted GPT-5.4. Aimless scrolling and waiting fall from 16.2%16.2\% to 5.5%5.5\%, with fewer repeated targets and dead-end probes. Figure 6 illustrates the difference. Verifying that Presenter Console is disabled requires a setting absent from the recorded trajectory. VeriCUA’s check names both the condition and its location (Tools →\rightarrow Options), and the Probe inspects it in two steps. Given the condition without the location, the Probe takes nine steps and never finds it.

3.4 Downstream Actor Learning

Actor performance.

Using VeriCUA rewards yields the highest Pass@44 among the compared reward sources on every split (Table 2). Overall Pass@44 rises from 43.93%43.93\% for the initial Actor to 47.14%47.14\%, a gain of 3.213.21 percentage points. On the MultiApp split, it rises from 17.57%17.57\% to 22.97%22.97\%, a gain of 5.405.40 percentage points. The Actor trained with prompted VeriCUA reaches 45.71%45.71\% overall and 20.27%20.27\% on MultiApp, below the corresponding results with the trained verifier.

Verification during Actor training.

To check whether this advantage persists as the Actor changes, we track verification behavior throughout the runs with prompted and trained VeriCUA rewards (details in Appendix H). With the trained verifier, agreement with executable outcomes is higher (81.4%81.4\% vs. 77.8%77.8\%), the false-negative rate is lower (4.6%4.6\% vs. 10.0%10.0\%), and the Probe-attempt rate is lower (4.28%4.28\% vs. 5.70%5.70\%). The trained verifier thus probes less often while missing fewer successes, consistent with a reward that scores both verdict correctness and Probe use.

4 Related Work

Reward signals for computer-use agents. Task-completion rewards for computer-use agents can be obtained from executable evaluators or model-based judgments. Executable evaluators derive outcome labels from application or backend state (Xie et al., 2024; Kong et al., 2026; El Hattami et al., 2025), relying on task-specific checking logic. Environment synthesis automates the construction of verifiable tasks by generating resettable tasks together with executable evaluators (Cao et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026b). Model-based evaluators assess recorded observations and action histories using prompted or trained judges (Bai et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025; Qi et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025; Xia et al., 2025), while rubric and milestone-based critics further structure this assessment (Rosset et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026). However, since recorded observations obscure uncaptured state, verifiers must acquire additional evidence through active interaction with the environment.

Interactive verification and evidence acquisition. Recent work incorporates evidence acquisition into both post-execution verification and task execution. Post-execution verifiers continue from the Actor’s terminal environment and inspect state before issuing a verdict (Dai et al., 2026; Cui et al., 2026; Shi et al., 2026). Other approaches integrate evidence collection, completeness checking, or recovery into the acting policy (Cai et al., 2025; Han et al., 2026). Text-reasoning verifiers can be trained with RL by replicating a problem to compare verification attempts (Zhang et al., 2026a); we study the post-execution GUI setting, where each state yields a single verification attempt.

5 Conclusion

We introduced VeriCUA, a proactive GUI reward agent that learns what to check and when to stop. Prompted verifiers benefit little from larger models or few-shot examples because a check’s value is revealed only through environment interaction. With only one verification attempt per Actor terminal state during training, VeriCUA learns this strategy by comparing outcomes across states. Across desktop, mobile, and web, it reaches the agreement–cost Pareto frontier, enables a 1B Judge to surpass prompted frontier models, and improves downstream policy RL. These results identify verification strategy, rather than model scale, as the key to reliable and affordable GUI reward supervision.

Reproducibility Statement

The interactive verification procedure and online training objective are specified in Sections 2.2 and 2.4. Section 3.1 describes the benchmark splits, baselines, and re-execution-based evaluation protocol. The appendix provides evaluation metrics, training and inference settings, the terminal reward schedule, and complete Judge and Probe prompts.

AI Use Statement

Large language model (LLM) tools were used in a supporting role to assist with coding and debugging in the reinforcement-learning framework, and to polish the manuscript’s writing for clarity and readability. Kimi-K2.6 was also used to generate candidate verification trajectories for the rejection-sampled SFT cold-start dataset. LLM tools were not used for brainstorming or generating research ideas. All AI-assisted textual edits were reviewed by the authors, and all AI-assisted code changes were reviewed and tested. The authors take full responsibility for the final content of this paper.

Appendix A Evaluation Metrics

For reward evaluation, let {(τi,Yi)}i=1N\{(\tau_{i},Y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N} be a set of Actor trajectories paired with executable evaluator outcomes. We run each verifier independently kk times on every trajectory and denote its jj-th verdict by Y^i,j\hat{Y}_{i,j}. Each proactive-verifier trial starts from a fresh re-execution of an accepted trajectory (Section 3.1). Passive verifiers score the fixed recorded observations. We report average agreement with the executable evaluator as

Avg@k=100N​k∑i=1N∑j=1k𝕀[Y^i,j=Yi].\mathrm{Avg@}k=\frac{100}{Nk}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{j=1}^{k}\mathbb{I}[\hat{Y}_{i,j}=Y_{i}]. (5)

Avg@kk thus measures how often verifier judgments match the executable outcome, not how often the Actor succeeds. ZeroGUI follows its official Majority@44 aggregation, as marked in Table 1.

For downstream Actor evaluation, let 𝒟\mathcal{D} be the task set and let Si,j∈{0,1}S_{i,j}\in\{0,1\} indicate whether the jj-th Actor rollout on task ii succeeds. We report the fraction of tasks solved at least once within kk rollouts as

Pass@k=100|𝒟|∑i∈𝒟𝕀[∑j=1kSi,j>0].\mathrm{Pass@}k=\frac{100}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}}\mathbb{I}\!\left[\sum_{j=1}^{k}S_{i,j}>0\right]. (6)

Both metrics are reported as percentages, and differences between them in percentage points.

Appendix B Behavioral Evidence for Targeted Verification

We analyze 33 OSWorld cases in which the recorded trajectory leaves the outcome-determining state unobserved, but the missing evidence can still be reached through the GUI. A correct verdict in these cases requires the Judge to find an effective verification path and to recognize when the returned evidence is sufficient.

Reward agreement and the Probe-budget ablation measure only the final verdict. To see how verification interaction is spent along the way, we measure four behavioral proxies (Table 3).

What the proxies capture.

Direct-evidence probes are Probe actions aimed at evidence that bears on task completion, so a higher rate means more specific checks. Aimless scrolling and waiting are actions that make no progress toward such evidence. Repeated targets count revisits to an already inspected target, and dead-end probes count exploration that never reaches useful evidence. Each proxy is computed independently over the same Probe interactions.

More focused evidence acquisition.

The trained verifier raises the direct-evidence rate by 14.3 points and cuts aimless scrolling and waiting by 10.7 points. Repeated targets and dead-end probes also decrease. Since the Probe is the same frozen model in both cases, these differences come from the checks the Judge issues.

Appendix C Reward Reliability across Probe Scales

Because the learned Judge decides what evidence to seek and the frozen Probe only executes the request, the two can be scaled separately. We hold the trained Judge, evaluation task set, and verification protocol fixed and vary only the Probe within the Holo3.1 family, from 35B-A3B to 9B and 4B. Each reported agreement aggregates repeated evaluation trials across multiple random seeds.

Sensitivity to Probe scale.

Agreement stays within 0.730.73 points across the three Probe models. The confidence intervals overlap closely, and agreement does not change monotonically with model size. Pairwise two-sample proportion tests give p=0.5843p=0.5843 (35B-A3B vs. 9B), p=0.9639p=0.9639 (35B-A3B vs. 4B), and p=0.6158p=0.6158 (9B vs. 4B). The 4B Probe reaches 82.07%82.07\%, against 82.00%82.00\% for 35B-A3B. Within the Holo3.1 family, the Probe can therefore be reduced to 4B without retraining the Judge.

Appendix D Evaluation Details

We use fixed inference settings for each component during reward evaluation. The Judge uses a sampling temperature of 1.01.0. The frozen Probe uses a sampling temperature of 0.00.0, a maximum output length of 81928192 tokens per API request, and at most 1515 interaction steps per probing round. The maximum number of probing rounds follows the main experimental setup (Section 3.1).

Trajectory screening and cost accounting.

We re-execute each Actor trajectory six times from the clean task snapshot and retain it only when all six re-executions yield the same executable outcome and the mean pHash similarity over their final three screenshots exceeds 0.950.95. Verifier trials then run in separate fresh re-executions. In cost accounting, trials that never call the Probe count as zero tokens, and image tokens follow Qwen-VL accounting. VAGEN has no separate Probe, so its full active loop is billed. We measure cost in Probe tokens because this is the cost the verification strategy controls. The Judge decides which checks the Probe executes and when probing stops. Within each benchmark, every prompted and trained VeriCUA Judge drives the same frozen Probe, so these tokens are counted on one model with one tokenizer. Judge tokens are not comparable in the same way. Tokenizers differ across backbones, closed models such as GPT-5.4 report reasoning only as provider-side counts, and per-token prices differ by orders of magnitude between a locally served 1B–4B model and a proprietary API. Counting Judge cost would therefore only widen the advantage of VeriCUA over proprietary Judge models.

The Judge is paired with an environment-specific frozen Probe. Within each benchmark, prompted and trained VeriCUA use the same Probe configuration, so any difference between them comes from the learned verification policy. Table 5 summarizes the default configurations.

Appendix E REINFORCE++ Optimization

We use the single-rollout REINFORCE++ estimator (Hu et al., 2025), as implemented in Slime. It assigns the terminal outcome reward to the generated Judge tokens in a complete verification rollout and normalizes their advantages globally, as in Equation 3. It therefore needs neither a same-state rollout group nor a learned value model. The main text states the underlying policy-gradient objective. Our implementation uses the standard PPO-style clipped surrogate:

ρi,k,t​(ϕ)\displaystyle\rho_{i,k,t}(\phi) =πϕJ​(yi,k,t∣hi,k,t)πoldJ​(yi,k,t∣hi,k,t),ρ¯i,k,t(ϕ)=clip(ρi,k,t(ϕ),1−ϵlow,1+ϵhigh),\displaystyle=\frac{\pi^{J}_{\phi}(y_{i,k,t}\mid h_{i,k,t})}{\pi^{J}_{\mathrm{old}}(y_{i,k,t}\mid h_{i,k,t})},\qquad\bar{\rho}_{i,k,t}(\phi)=\operatorname{clip}\!\left(\rho_{i,k,t}(\phi),1-\epsilon_{\mathrm{low}},1+\epsilon_{\mathrm{high}}\right), (7)
ℒclip​(ϕ)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{clip}}(\phi) =−1|𝒜ℬ|∑(i,k,t)∈𝒜ℬmin{ρi,k,t(ϕ)Ai,k,t,ρ¯i,k,t(ϕ)Ai,k,t}.\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{B}}|}\sum_{(i,k,t)\in\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{B}}}\min\!\left\{\rho_{i,k,t}(\phi)A_{i,k,t},\bar{\rho}_{i,k,t}(\phi)A_{i,k,t}\right\}.

Appendix F Implementation Details

Training implementation.

We implement cold-start Judge SFT using LLaMA-Factory. The Qwen3-VL-4B Judge is fine-tuned on eight GPUs with DeepSpeed ZeRO-3. Online RL uses Slime with Megatron Core for parameter updates and SGLang for rollout generation. For online Judge RL, we allocate eight NVIDIA A800-SXM4 GPUs (80 GB each) to parameter updates and eight additional GPUs to rollout generation. Parameter updates use eight-way tensor parallelism, and rollout generation uses single-GPU engines. Training uses BF16 precision. Objectives and hyperparameters are given in Appendices E and G.

Inference implementation.

We also run Judge and Probe inference on Huawei Ascend 910B3 accelerators. The eight-NPU configuration comprises three Probe instances using two NPUs each and two Judge instances using one NPU each. Inference uses BF16 precision with vLLM 0.18.0 and vLLM-Ascend 0.18.0, running on CANN 9.0.0, PyTorch 2.9.0, and torch-npu 2.9.0.post2. Model inference and GUI execution run in separate processes and communicate through API requests. Model choices and decoding settings are given in Appendix D.

Desktop environments.

The Ascend-based desktop evaluation uses 16 independent x86 Ubuntu 22.04.3 virtual machines at a resolution of 1920×10801920\times 1080, each with four virtual CPUs and 4 GiB of memory. The virtual machines run under QEMU 8.2.10 with TCG emulation on ARM64 hosts. Environment initialization, trajectory re-execution, and verifier isolation follow the protocol in Appendix D.

Appendix G VeriCUA Training Details

Cold-start Judge SFT.

We use the same cold-start SFT procedure for the Qwen3-VL-2B-Thinking, Qwen3-VL-4B-Thinking, and MiniCPM-V-4.6-Thinking Judge backbones. Each backbone is fully SFT-tuned on approximately 1,2701{,}270 Kimi-K2.6 verification traces retained by the rejection-sampling procedure in Section 2.4. These traces are generated over OSWorld trajectories from EvoCUA-32B, Holo3.1-35B-A3B, Qwen3-VL-4B-Thinking, and Qwen3.6-27B. The vision tower and multimodal projector remain frozen while the language model is updated. Previous assistant turns serve only as context, and the loss is applied to the current assistant turn. Thinking content from earlier turns is removed during data construction.

Online VeriCUA training.

Table 7 summarizes the training protocol shared by the Qwen3-VL-2B-Thinking, Qwen3-VL-4B-Thinking, and MiniCPM-V-4.6-Thinking Judge backbones. The OSWorld training set, Actor pool, Probe, verification budget, RL objective, and optimization configuration are identical across backbones.

Downstream Actor RL.

All downstream reward-source comparisons start from the same Qwen3-VL-4B-Thinking Actor and use the same training tasks, rollout budget, GRPO objective, and optimization configuration. Only the reward provider changes. When VeriCUA supplies the rewards, both the learned Judge and the Holo3.1 Probe are frozen. Table 8 lists the shared settings.

Terminal reward.

Probe usage is binary: pi=1p_{i}=1 if rollout ziz_{i} contains at least one Probe invocation, regardless of the number of Judge–Probe rounds. All rewards use the executable outcome YiY_{i} recorded before Probe interaction. The exact schedule is given in Table 9.

An output counts as unresolved or invalid if the final decision is uncertain, the output cannot be parsed, or the executable evaluator returns no metadata. Under this schedule, a correct verdict is worth more without probing, while a wrong verdict costs less after probing, so the reward favors probing exactly when the screenshot-only verdict is likely to be wrong.

Appendix H Verification Behavior during Downstream Actor RL

We log every Judge decision from two downstream Actor-RL runs, one rewarded by prompted VeriCUA and the other by trained VeriCUA. The runs share the initial Actor, tasks, rollout budget, and optimization configuration. Comparing their decisions with executable outcomes shows how verification behaves as the Actor changes. Tables 10 and 7 report how often the Judge probes, how reliably its Probe requests are dispatched, and how often its verdicts match the executable outcome.

Dispatch failures and unresolved verdicts.

Failed Probe dispatch falls from 16.6%16.6\% to 3.2%3.2\%, and unresolved uncertain outputs fall from 1.9%1.9\% to 0.4%0.4\% (Figure 7(a)). The Probe is frozen in both runs, so the improvement comes from the Judge. It learns to issue checks that the Probe can act on and to reach a terminal decision from the returned evidence. It does so with 25%25\% fewer Probe attempts (Table 10).

Agreement over the course of Actor training.

VeriCUA leads prompted VeriCUA in agreement by 4.24.2 points in the first half of training and 3.23.2 points in the second (Figure 7(b)). Its false-negative rate is also lower (4.6%4.6\% vs. 10.0%10.0\%), so fewer successful Actor rollouts receive a zero reward.
